title: How to Improve School Cultures, Part 3: Better Meetings
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that school culture is built not only by how leaders lead but by how staffs meet. He borrows Seth Godin's seven-item checklist for deciding whether a meeting is worth holding and tests it against the reality of school calendars, where a single monthly whole-staff hour is crammed with competing agendas. His move is to treat that overload as the default symptom of people doing too much, and to prescribe a culture that ruthlessly eliminates pointless tasks and satisfices on the rest. He proposes a start-of-year meeting devoted to naming and minimizing pointless work, and ends by teeing up argument as the thing that makes meetings worth attending.
points: Godin's checklist (one responsible person, matched time, right invitees, stated desired outcome, advance materials) is offered as a practical test of whether a meeting should exist.
Contract-defined school calendars make the checklist hard to meet, so cram-everything monthly staff meetings are the predictable default rather than a failure of individual leaders.
The deeper fix is cultural: eliminate pointless tasks outright and satisfice on those that cannot be eliminated, so time is protected for what matters most.
A first-of-year staff meeting to brainstorm pointless work would itself pass Godin's test, because no better way exists to create shared understanding about minimizing it.
Meetings are worth attending when they host real argument, a thread Stuart sets up for the next post.
quotes: If we want to improve the cultures of our schools, we'd be smart to look not just at the way we lead, but also the way we meet. Whether meeting one-on-one or as a whole district, informally or formally, as a PLC or as a grade-level team, meetings create culture.

First, it's tricky for school meetings, especially at the whole-staff level, to meet all of these requirements. In plenty of schools, meetings are dictated by contract-defined school calendars. When you only get a single one-hour meeting with the whole staff per month, there's bound to be more than one person responsible, and there's bound to be so much to talk about that you'll cram a month's worth of things into the allotted time frame.
The preceding paragraph is the default for meetings in schools. It's what happens when all of us are doing too much.

This is why, in the best schools, leaders work to do what matters most while minimizing or eliminating time spent on everything else. This is at the root of making meetings the kinds of things that improve school cultures. We need to build cultures that ruthlessly eliminate pointless tasks; for tasks that can't be eliminated, we need to satisfice.

There should probably be a whole meeting at the start of each year where a staff brainstorms pointless things and creates shared understanding for how to strategically minimize time spent on these things. The desired outcome? Give ourselves space to do better, saner work.

Arguments, after all, make meetings worth attending. It may seem counterintuitive in an age where we can't seem to argue amicably in the public square, but that's just because we're not doing argument right.
